Tarlow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Tarłów, Poland

Not demolished. Tarłów, founded by Andrzej Tarła on the site of the former royal staging-post village Czekarzewice and granted Magdeburg rights in 1550, exempted its residents from taxes for two decades. Jews settled almost immediately, owning a wooden synagogue and this cemetery by 1609; a 1665 privilege from Jan Oleśnicki confirms a funeral house also stood on the grounds. By 1787, Jews made up 49.3% of the population; Russian forces burned the synagogue and much of the Jewish quarter during WWI, though the community still comprised roughly half the town's residents by the interwar period (1,800 by 1937). A 1941 ghetto held about 10,000 Jews from Tarłów and the surrounding Starachowice district; roughly 8,000 were deported to Treblinka in 1942. During the war, the cemetery itself was used for executions; postwar, locals repurposed the remaining tombstone material for construction. In 2011, descendant Jan Curyła led a cleanup and fencing effort, unveiling a monument with recovered tombstones gathered around it; a 2019 field survey identified 32 mostly broken sandstone matzevot dating from 1787 to 1896, alongside a surviving cemetery road and ditch mentioned in the original 1665 privilege.
